a: In the second year of Darius's reign
t: A date Ezra gives one verse earlier
p: Ezra dates the restart at the end of chapter 4; 1 Esdras puts the date at the head of the prophets' work.
b:
Ezra 5:1 has no date of its own: the date stands at the end of the previous chapter, where the work stops "until the second year of the reign of Darius" (Ezra 4:24). 1 Esdras has already told that stop at 2:25, and here it moves the date into the first line of the new story. Haggai and Zechariah date their first messages to the same year: "the second year of King Darius" (Haggai 1:1) and "the second year of Darius" (Zechariah 1:1).

In 1 Esdras this Darius is also the king of the three guards' contest (3:1-4:63), so in this book's order the rebuilding follows straight from Zerubbabel's win at court. See the chapter page.

p: The Greek spells Iddo as Eddein; Codex Alexandrinus has Addo.
b: Vaticanus, the codex Swete prints, has Eddein; Swete's footnote gives Addo for Alexandrinus, and the KJV follows that ("Zacharias the son of Addo"). Both are forms of the Hebrew name Iddo (Ezra 5:1; Zechariah 1:1 calls him the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo). The Plain uses the name readers know.

p: The Greek uses the name of the Persian and Greek province, Ioudaia.
b: Where Ezra's Aramaic has Yehud, "Judah," 1 Esdras uses Ioudaia, the name the province had in the Persian and Greek periods. The Plain keeps "Judea" all through this book. The KJV's "Jewry" is an older English name for the same place.

a: The Lord's prophets were with them, helping them
t: The prophets who urged the building
p: Haggai and Zechariah both spoke to Zerubbabel and Jeshua about the house.
b: Haggai's first message is addressed to "Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest" (Haggai 1:1), and it blames the people for living in finished houses while the Lord's house lies in ruins (Haggai 1:4). Zechariah promises that Zerubbabel's hands, which laid the foundation, will finish it (Zechariah 4:9). 1 Esdras shortens Ezra here, but it keeps the picture of prophets working beside the builders.

a: Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia
p: Ezra calls the governor Tattenai, of "Beyond the River"; 1 Esdras calls him Sisinnes, of Syria and Phoenicia.
b: In Ezra 5:3 the official is Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, the Persian province west of the Euphrates. 1 Esdras names him Sisinnes and his colleague Sathrabuzanes (Ezra's Shethar-bozenai), and calls the province "Syria and Phoenicia," a name of the Greek period (2 Maccabees 3:5 has "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia"). The roles and the story are the same, so the same officials are meant, whatever the reason for the different name.

p: Vaticanus spells the colleague Sathrabuzanes here and Sathrabourzanes at 6:7.
b: Swete prints Vaticanus as it stands, and Vaticanus is not consistent: Sathrabouzanes here and at 6:26, Sathrabourzanes at 6:7. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with Sathrabouzanes at 6:7. The Plain uses one spelling throughout. Ezra has Shethar-bozenai.

p: Ezra's hard Aramaic word for the work becomes "this roof" in 1 Esdras.
b:
In Ezra 5:3 the officials ask who allowed the Jews "to build this house and complete these fittings." The Aramaic word behind "fittings" ('ussarna) is rare and its meaning is debated: a wall, a structure, or the fittings of the building. 1 Esdras has "this roof" (stegē). Either way the question is the same: by whose permission are you building?

1 Esdras also smooths a puzzle in Ezra 5:4, where the Aramaic says "Then we said to them." Here the officials ask both questions, and no "we" appears.

a: because the Lord had come to watch over the captives
p: Ezra says "their God kept his eye on the elders"; the Greek says the Lord paid a visit to the captives.
b: The Aramaic of Ezra 5:5 has "the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews." 1 Esdras uses episkopē, the word for an overseer's visit, which the Greek Bible often uses for God coming to look after his people (Genesis 50:24 in Greek; Luke 1:68 uses the verb). The meaning is close, but the Greek ties the favor to the exiles as a whole, "the captivity," rather than to the elders alone.

p: The letter opens with chairein, the ordinary greeting of Greek letters.
b: Ezra's Aramaic letter opens "To Darius the king: all peace" (Ezra 5:7). 1 Esdras uses the Greek letter formula "To King Darius, chairein," the same greeting that opens the letter of the Jerusalem council and the letter of James (Acts 15:23; James 1:1). It is one of many signs that the book was shaped for Greek readers.

p: In Ezra the word "great" can go with God; in 1 Esdras it describes the house.
b: The Aramaic of Ezra 5:8 says the officials went "to the house of the great God," though the phrase can also be read "the great house of God." The site's Ezra follows the first. 1 Esdras takes it the second way, and goes further: the Jews are building "a house for the Lord, great and new." So the Persian officials' report becomes a report about an impressive building project, which fits the worry of a provincial governor.

p: The Greek uses aichmalosia, captivity, where Ezra uses golah, the exile.
b: 1 Esdras calls the returned community "the captivity" (aichmalōsia) or "those from the captivity." It stands where Ezra's Hebrew and Aramaic have golah, "the exile," and the Plain renders the phrase "the people of the exile," as in Ezra (Ezra 6:16; 10:7). The Greek word keeps the memory of being carried off by force; the Hebrew word stresses having been sent away.

p: Ezra has "servants of the God of the heavens and the earth"; 1 Esdras makes him their creator.
b: Ezra 5:11 calls the elders "servants of the God of the heavens and the earth," the title the Persian court used for Israel's God. 1 Esdras turns it into a confession: the Lord "who created heaven and earth," the language of Genesis 1:1 and of the Psalms (Psalm 121:2; Psalm 124:8). Before a Persian governor, the elders name their God as the maker of everything, including Persia.

a: A great and strong king of Israel
p: The king who built the first house was Solomon; neither Ezra nor 1 Esdras names him.
b: Both Ezra 5:11 and this verse leave Solomon unnamed, as if the elders speak in the plain terms a Persian official would follow. 1 Esdras adds "strong" to "great." The first temple was finished in Solomon's eleventh year (1 Kings 6:38) and burned by Nebuchadnezzar's army (2 Kings 25:9).

p: Ezra says the house was torn down; 1 Esdras adds that it was burned.
b: Ezra 5:12 says only that Nebuchadnezzar "tore down this house." 1 Esdras adds the fire, as in 2 Kings 25:9 and 2 Chronicles 36:19, and makes the destroyers plural, "they." The change fits the book's opening, which told the burning at 1:52.

a: They were given to Zerubbabel and to Sanabassar the governor
p: Ezra gives the vessels to Sheshbazzar alone; 1 Esdras names Zerubbabel first.
b:
In Ezra 5:14 the vessels go to "Sheshbazzar, as he was called, the man he had made governor." 1 Esdras names two men, Zerubbabel and Sanabassar (its form of Sheshbazzar), with Zerubbabel first. This matches the book's larger story, in which Zerubbabel is the hero who wins the king's favor (4:42-57). But it creates a tension: the next two verses go on speaking of one man, and only Sanabassar lays the foundation (6:19).

Who Sheshbazzar was, and whether he and Zerubbabel are one person, is an old question; see the topic page.

p: The Greek name stands for the Sheshbazzar of Ezra, spelled two ways in Vaticanus.
b: Vaticanus spells the name Sabanassaros here and Sanabassaros at 6:19; Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with Sanabassaros in both places, and the KJV has "Sanabassarus." The Plain uses the form of 6:19 without its Greek ending. Ezra's Hebrew and Aramaic have Sheshbazzar.

p: Ezra says to search the treasure house; 1 Esdras says the royal archives.
b: Ezra 5:17 asks for a search "in the king's treasure house," and Ezra 6:1 speaks of a house of records where treasures were stored. 1 Esdras uses bibliophylakia, "places where books are kept," for both (also 6:22). The Greek makes plain what the search is for: a written record.

a: Ecbatana, the fortress in the land of Media
p: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran, was the old city of the Medes.
b: Ecbatana, today Hamadan in western Iran, was the city of the Medes; Judith 1:1 has a king of the Medes ruling there. Ezra 6:1-2 says Darius had the house of records in Babylon searched and that the scroll was found at Ecbatana, and 1 Esdras tells it the same way, with "archives" for the house of records. Neither book says why a copy of Cyrus's order was kept at Ecbatana.

a: with fire that never goes out
p: Ezra says only that it is a place of sacrifice; 1 Esdras adds the never-ending fire of Leviticus.
b: Ezra 6:3 says the house is "to be built as a place where sacrifices are offered." 1 Esdras adds that they sacrifice "through continual fire" (pyros endelechous), the language of the law that the altar fire must never go out (Leviticus 6:12-13). In a Persian king's memo the phrase reads oddly, which suggests the translator's own piety at work.

a: sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide
t: A house as tall as it is wide
p: The decree gives height and width but no length, in 1 Esdras as in Ezra.
b: Sixty cubits is about 90 feet (27 meters). Solomon's temple was thirty cubits high and twenty wide (1 Kings 6:2), so the figures are either a maximum the king allowed or a corrupted text. 1 Esdras has the same two numbers as Ezra 6:3 and, like it, no length. The older people who remembered the first house wept at how small the new one looked (Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3), which does not fit a building larger than Solomon's.

p: Ezra says the cost comes from "the king's house"; 1 Esdras names Cyrus.
b: Ezra 6:4 orders the cost to be paid "out of the king's house," that is, the royal treasury. 1 Esdras names it the house of King Cyrus. Then in 6:28 Darius adds his own grant from the tribute of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. For Cyrus himself, and his own inscription, the Cyrus Cylinder, see the topic page.

p: The scroll's words end, and an order follows in the third person: is it Cyrus or Darius?
b: In Ezra 6:6 the voice turns without warning from Cyrus's memo to Darius's own reply ("Now, Tattenai..."). 1 Esdras reports that turn as narration: "He also ordered Sisinnes..." Grammatically the "he" could still be Cyrus, but Sisinnes is Darius's governor, so the context points to Darius. The next verse confirms it: "I also have given orders," Darius speaking in the first person (6:27-33). The Plain closes Cyrus's memo at 6:25 and opens Darius's words at 6:27.

p: Only 1 Esdras puts this title on Zerubbabel, and it puts it in a Persian order.
b: Ezra 6:7 speaks only of "the Jews' governor." 1 Esdras names him: Zerubbabel, pais Kyriou, "the Lord's servant." The title echoes Haggai's last oracle, where the LORD says, "I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant" (Haggai 2:23). It is the language used of Moses, David and the servant of Isaiah 40-55. In a decree of Darius it is surprising; it shows how far 1 Esdras raises Zerubbabel, the winner of the three guards' contest.

p: Sisinnes is the eparch; Zerubbabel is the hyparch, the governor beneath him.
b: The Greek gives the two men different titles. Sisinnes is the eparchos, governor of the large province; Zerubbabel is the hyparchos of Judea, a governor under him. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with a different word here. In 6:28 Zerubbabel is called simply "the governor." Haggai calls him "governor of Judah" (Haggai 1:1), using the Persian title pechah.

p: Coele-Syria is a name from the Greek period, and it helps date the book.
b: Coele-Syria, "Hollow Syria," is a name of the Greek period. 2 Maccabees uses it for the province of Apollonius, "governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia" (2 Maccabees 3:5; 2 Maccabees 4:4). In Ezra the province is "Beyond the River." A Persian decree would hardly use the Greek name, so the term belongs to the translator and his readers.

p: Ezra's "God of the heavens" becomes "the Most High God" in 1 Esdras.
b: The Aramaic of Ezra 6:10 has "the God of the heavens," the title Persian documents use. 1 Esdras uses ho theos ho hypsistos, "God Most High," a title Greek-speaking Jews favored because it was understood by their neighbors too (Genesis 14:18 in Greek; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17). It recurs in Artaxerxes' letter (8:19, 8:21) and at the reading of the law (9:46).
orig: τῷ θεῷ τῷ ὑψίστῳ (tō theō tō hypsistō)

a: be hanged on it, and his property is to go to the king
p: Ezra adds that the man's house becomes a dunghill; 1 Esdras has the property go to the king.
b: Ezra 6:11 says the offender is to be "lifted up and impaled" on a beam from his house, and "his house is to be made a dunghill." 1 Esdras has "hanged" (kremasthēnai) and orders his property seized for the king, with no dunghill.

a: whose name is called on there
p: Ezra says God made his name live there; 1 Esdras says his name is called on there.
b: Ezra 6:12 uses Deuteronomy's language of the place where God makes his name dwell (Deuteronomy 12:11). 1 Esdras uses another biblical phrase, the house "called by my name" or over which the Lord's name is called (1 Kings 8:43; Jeremiah 7:10-11). Both say that the temple belongs to Israel's God, so that harming it is an attack on him.

p: A new group appears: the Persian officials work with the elders and the hierostatai.
b: Ezra 6:13-14 has the officials obey and the elders build. 1 Esdras turns the Persian officials into supervisors of the "holy works," working with the elders of the Jews and hierostatai, "temple overseers," a word found only here in the Greek Bible. The picture is of a government project with Jewish and royal officers side by side.

t: Artaxerxes in a list about Darius
p: Artaxerxes reigned after Darius, so his name here looks ahead.
b: Ezra 6:14 also lists Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes, though the house was finished under Darius, in his sixth year (7:5). Artaxerxes came later: Josephus has Xerxes succeed Darius (Antiquities 11.120), and it is an Artaxerxes who sends Ezra with gifts for the temple (8:8-24). The list seems to sum up the Persian kings who helped the temple. 1 Esdras, which already set an Artaxerxes letter before Darius's reign (2:15-25), keeps the list as it stands.

a: by the twenty-third day of the month of Adar
p: Ezra 6:15 has the third of Adar; 1 Esdras and Josephus have the twenty-third.
b: The Hebrew text of Ezra 6:15 gives the third day of Adar, the twelfth month, in Darius's sixth year. 1 Esdras has the twenty-third. Josephus also has "the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, which is by us called Adar," but in Darius's ninth year (Antiquities 11.107). The Greek wording here, "until the twenty-third" (heōs tritēs kai eikados), can also mean the work went on up to that day.

a: acted as the book of Moses directs
p: Ezra says they held the dedication joyfully; 1 Esdras says they acted by the book of Moses.
b: Ezra 6:16 says the people "joyfully held the dedication of this house of God." 1 Esdras leaves out the joy here and says instead that everyone did what is in the book of Moses, a phrase Ezra uses two verses later (Ezra 6:18). The joy comes back at the Feast of Unleavened Bread (7:14). The change puts the law at the center from the first day of the new temple.

a: 12 male goats as a sin offering for all Israel
p: Though most of the returnees were from Judah and Benjamin, the offering stands for all twelve tribes.
b: The number matches "Israel's tribal leaders, twelve." The returnees came mostly from Judah, Benjamin and Levi (Ezra 1:5), yet the offering is made for the whole people, as if the northern tribes were still present before God. Twelve bulls and twelve goats are offered again when Ezra arrives (8:63). Jesus' choice of twelve disciples draws on the same hope of all Israel gathered again (Matthew 19:28).

p: The Greek says the priests and Levites stood by tribes, where Ezra has their divisions and groups.
b: Ezra 6:18 says the priests were installed "by their divisions" and the Levites "by their groups," the duty rosters of 1 Chronicles 23-26. 1 Esdras has kata phylas, "by tribes," a loose word for these family groups, and pictures them "robed" and standing over the work. It also adds the gatekeepers at every gate, a detail Ezra does not give here.

a: For the Levites had all been made pure together
p: The Greek repeats itself here, probably from a copying or translation slip.
b: The Greek of 7:10-11 says twice that the priests and Levites were purified. It reads as if two forms of Ezra 6:20 were run together: "the priests and the Levites had made themselves pure together" and "the Levites were all purified." The KJV keeps both clauses. The point is the same as in Ezra: those who slaughtered the Passover were ritually clean.

a: all who had separated themselves from the abhorrent practices of the nations of the land
p: In Ezra outsiders who separate themselves can join; in 1 Esdras the separated are the returnees themselves.
b:
Ezra 6:21 says the returned exiles ate the Passover "along with everyone who had separated himself to them from the uncleanness of the nations of the land." Those people may be converts, or Judeans who had never been exiled, who now joined the community. 1 Esdras drops "along with" and "to them": the people who separated themselves are the exiles. The Greek reading leaves no room for newcomers and fits the strict line of the marriage story in chapters 8-9.

The Greek also has "abhorrent practices" (bdelygmata) where Ezra 6:21 has "uncleanness"; "abhorrent practices" is the site's word in Ezra 9:1.

p: The capitals follow the Hebrew parallel; the Greek has the same word, kyrios, for both.
b: The Greek of 1 Esdras has one word, kyrios, "Lord," for God throughout. The Plain prints "the LORD" in capitals only where the parallel verse of Ezra or Nehemiah has the Hebrew name of God (here Ezra 6:21, "to seek the LORD") and the Greek has kyrios there; elsewhere it prints "the Lord." So in 7:14-15, 8:57 or 9:52 the capitals change within a few words although the Greek does not. See the note on 1:1.

p: The ruler of Persia is called the king of Assyria, as in Ezra 6:22.
b: 1 Esdras keeps Ezra's surprising title. Persian kings ruled the old lands of Assyria, and Judith gives the title just as loosely when it calls Nebuchadnezzar the king "who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (Judith 1:1). The Greek boulē, "will, plan," stands for Ezra's "heart."

p: Ezra arrives under Artaxerxes, at least a whole reign after the temple was finished.
b: Between Darius, who saw the temple finished (7:5), and Artaxerxes came Xerxes: Josephus says Xerxes succeeded Darius, and he puts Ezra under Xerxes instead (Antiquities 11.120-121). 1 Esdras, like Ezra 7:1, passes over the years between without a word. It also has no Nehemiah, whose memoir is set in the twentieth year of a King Artaxerxes (Nehemiah 2:1). Which Artaxerxes sent Ezra is discussed on the topic page.

a: son of Zechrias, son of Helkias, son of Salemus
p: The Greek list differs from Ezra 7:1-5 in spelling and leaves out three names.
b: Ezra 7:1-5 traces Ezra to Aaron through Seraiah, Azariah, Hilkiah, Shallum, Zadok, Ahitub, Amariah, Azariah, Meraioth, Zerahiah, Uzzi, Bukki, Abishua, Phinehas and Eleazar. Vaticanus begins with Azaraias (Swete's footnote gives Saraias for Alexandrinus, Ezra's Seraiah) and lacks the stretch Azariah-Meraioth-Zerahiah, which Alexandrinus has (see the variant at 8:2). The Greek forms here: Zechrias for Azariah, Helkias for Hilkiah, Salemus for Shallum, Saddulukus for Zadok, Amartheus for Amariah, Ozeias for Uzzi, Bokkas for Bukki, Abisai for Abishua. The Plain follows the Greek.

p: Ezra has "the head priest"; the Greek says "the first priest."
b: The Hebrew of Ezra 7:5 calls Aaron hakkohen haro'sh, "the head priest." The Greek prōtos can mean either "first in rank" or "first in time," and both are true of Aaron. Alexandrinus reverses the words but keeps the sense.

p: Ezra has "an expert"; the Greek euphyes means naturally gifted.
b: In Ezra 7:6 the Hebrew calls Ezra a sofer mahir, a skilled scribe, literally a quick one. The Greek euphyēs means "well-grown, naturally gifted, clever." It makes Ezra's skill a matter of talent as well as training. 1 Esdras also drops "Because the LORD his God's hand was on him" from the next clause (8:4) and gives the king's favor as the reason for his success.

p: The Greek hierodouloi means temple slaves; Ezra has the netinim, the "given ones."
b: The Plain renders the Hebrew netinim as "temple servants" everywhere, with a note on the word, "given ones" (Ezra 2:43). 1 Esdras uses hierodouloi, "sacred slaves," a Greek word for workers attached to a temple. The Plain uses the same English for both, but the Greek reader would hear a lower status than "given ones" suggests.

p: Ezra says he set his heart to search out, do and teach the law; 1 Esdras praises his great knowledge.
b: Ezra 7:10 is a much-loved verse: Ezra "had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law, to doing it, and to teaching" it. 1 Esdras turns the three steps into one quality: Ezra "had much knowledge" (epistēmē), so that he left out nothing. The Greek portrait is of a learned man; the Hebrew stresses his heart and his practice. Swete's Vaticanus here even calls him "Apsarus" (see the variant).

p: Throughout 1 Esdras Ezra is the anagnostes, the "reader," of the law.
b: Ezra's title in Hebrew and Aramaic is sofer, "scribe." 1 Esdras calls him anagnōstēs, "reader," in the king's letter (8:8-9, 8:19) and at the great reading (9:39, 9:42, 9:49), but keeps grammateus, "scribe," at 8:3. In Greek cities the anagnōstēs was the man who read texts aloud, and in the church the word became the name of the order of Reader. The Greek title fits the book's climax, the public reading of the law.

a: I have decided on acts of kindness
p: The king speaks the language of Hellenistic royal grants: philanthropa, "kind acts."
b: Ezra 7:13 opens with "A decree goes out from me." 1 Esdras has ta philanthrōpa, "the kind things," a set phrase in the decrees of the Ptolemies and Seleucids for royal favors and privileges granted to a city or a people (compare 2 Maccabees 4:11). Readers in the Greek world would recognize a charter of rights.

p: The Persian king had seven chief advisers; 1 Esdras calls them "Friends," a Greek court title.
b: Ezra 7:14 speaks of "the king and his seven counselors," and Esther 1:14 names "the seven officials of Persia and Media," who "had the right to see the king face to face." 1 Esdras calls them "Friends" (philoi), the rank title of the Hellenistic courts, as when a king lists Jonathan "among the First Friends" (1 Maccabees 10:65). The Plain capitalizes Friends here as a title.

t: Measures of wine, no oil or salt
p: The Greek uses the Greek liquid measure and leaves out Ezra's oil and salt.
b: Ezra 7:22 gives 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of olive oil, and salt without limit. The Greek has 100 kors of wheat and 100 metrētai of wine, a Greek liquid measure, and stops there. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus adding "and other things in abundance."

p: Ezra may appoint judges for all the Jews of the province who know the law of God.
b: As in Ezra 7:25, the king gives Ezra authority over "everyone who knows your God's law" in the whole western province, and tells him to teach those who do not. The law of Moses is made royal law for the Jews of the region (8:24).

a: into my heart, the king's heart
p: In Vaticanus the blessing seems to run on from the king's letter; in Alexandrinus Ezra speaks it.
b: In Ezra 7:27 the letter ends and Ezra breaks into praise: "Blessed is the LORD, God of our ancestors!" Vaticanus has no break and no speaker: "Blessed alone is the Lord, who gave these things into my heart, of the king." Read as it stands, the king himself might be blessing the Lord. The next verse shows Ezra speaking ("He has honored me"). Alexandrinus adds "And Ezra the scribe said" and lacks "my," which gives Ezra's sense (see the variant). The Plain keeps Vaticanus and its awkward "my."

a: Of the descendants of Ietamarus, Gamelus
p: Vaticanus's first names hardly resemble Ezra's Phinehas and Gershom.
b: Ezra 8:2 begins: "Of the descendants of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the descendants of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the descendants of David, Hattush." In Vaticanus, Phinehas has become Phoros (the Greek form of Parosh, the lay family of Ezra 8:3), Gershom has become Tarosotomus, and Daniel Gamelus. Even the first letter of Tarosotomus is unsure: the digital texts of Swete print it with T or with G, and the lemma of his footnote has R (Rarosotomos). Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus closer to the Hebrew: Phinees, Gerson, Ithamar, Iamael. The Plain follows Swete's text and gives the readings in the variants.

p: Without Hattush, the line reads as if Zechariah were from David's line through "Phares."
b: In Ezra 8:2-3 Hattush is "of the descendants of David" and Zechariah is "of the descendants of Parosh." Vaticanus lacks Hattush, so "Phares" follows David directly. A Greek reader could take it as Perez (Greek Phares), David's ancestor (Ruth 4:18; Matthew 1:3), but it is most likely a form of Parosh, as Alexandrinus's "of the sons of Phoros" shows. The Plain keeps the Greek.

p: Several figures in 1 Esdras differ from Ezra 8.
b: Compared with Ezra 8:3-14: Zathoes (Zattu) has 200 men for 300 (Swete's footnote gives 300 for Alexandrinus); Adin has 250 for 50; Sophotias (Shephatiah) 70 for 80; Joab 212 for 218; Adonikam 70 for 60. Ezra's total is 1,496 men; the figures in Vaticanus here add up to 1,590. Number words were easily miscopied, and neither list can be checked against outside evidence.

p: Ezra names the river that runs to Ahava; Vaticanus says only "the so-called River."
b: Ezra 8:15 gathers the people "by the river that runs to Ahava." Vaticanus has "at the so-called River," and Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus adding a name before "River" (Theran): "the river called Thera." At 8:60 the departure is "from the place Thera" (Alexandrinus there has "the river"). Ahava is unknown outside Ezra; Josephus says only that they "removed from Euphrates on the twelfth day of the first month" (Antiquities 11.135).

a: Finding none of the priests or the Levites there
p: In Ezra only the Levites are missing; in 1 Esdras the priests are missing too.
b: Ezra 8:15 says Ezra looked over "the people and the priests" and found no descendant of Levi. Priests are already in the company (Ezra 8:2). 1 Esdras says he found none "of the priests or of the Levites," and in 8:45 he asks for men "to serve as priests." Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with "of the sons of the priests." The Greek seems to have lost the contrast that makes Ezra's point: the priests came, but the Levites, who did the heavier temple work, held back.

a: the head man at the Treasury
p: The Greek translates the place name Casiphia as "the place of the treasury."
b: Ezra 8:17 sends the men to Iddo, "the head man at the place called Casiphia." The name Kasifya looks like the Hebrew kesef, "silver, money," and 1 Esdras renders it "the place of the treasury" (gazophylakion). The leader's name, Iddo, appears as Laadaeus here and as Lodaeus in 8:45 (Swete's footnote gives Doldaeus for Alexandrinus in both).

a: Asebebias, with his sons and brothers, ten
p: Vaticanus gives ten; Ezra and Alexandrinus give eighteen.
b: Ezra 8:18 names Sherebiah of the line of Mahli, with his sons and brothers, 18 in all. Vaticanus has Asebebias and "ten." The sentence in Vaticanus also lacks Ezra's "Our God's good hand was on us, and so they brought us," so the names depend on "to send us" in 8:45 (see the variant). Sherebiah becomes one of the twelve trusted with the treasure (8:54, Eserebias) and stands among the Levites at the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8:7.

t: A fast for the young men?
p: Ezra calls a fast "to humble ourselves"; the Greek says "for the young men."
b: In Ezra 8:21 the purpose of the fast is that "We were to humble ourselves before our God" (Hebrew lehit'annot). 1 Esdras says Ezra vowed a fast tois neaniskois, "for the young men," which has no clear source in the Hebrew we have. The young men may be the fighting-age men who would have been the escort, or the Greek may reflect a different or misread Hebrew text. The KJV keeps "for the young men."

a: to set everything right for them
p: Ezra's words to the king include God's anger on those who abandon him; 1 Esdras keeps only the promise.
b: Ezra 8:22 records the claim Ezra made to the king: "Our God's hand is on everyone who seeks him, for their good. But his strength and his anger are against everyone who abandons him." 1 Esdras has only the first half, with "the strength of our Lord" now on the side of those who seek him. The bold boast that made Ezra ashamed to ask for soldiers (8:51) is still there; the warning is gone.

a: ten vessels of fine, gleaming bronze
p: Ezra lists two bronze vessels; Vaticanus has ten, Alexandrinus twelve.
b: Ezra 8:27 has 20 gold bowls worth 1,000 darics and two vessels of gleaming bronze, "as costly as gold." 1 Esdras has 20 chrysōmata, "gold articles," which the Plain does not turn into Ezra's bowls; it leaves out their value and has ten bronze vessels; Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with twelve "gold-like" ones, and without the 100 talents of gold (see the variant). A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so 650 talents of silver would be about 22 tons, an enormous sum whichever text one follows.

a: You also are holy to the LORD
p: Only people set apart to God may carry the things set apart to God.
b: Ezra's charge to the priests rests on the law that holy things belong in holy hands (Numbers 4:15; Numbers 18:3). The gifts are now the Lord's, and the carriers share their status for the journey. 1 Esdras calls the silver and gold a "vow" (euchē), something promised to God, where Ezra 8:28 has a freewill offering.

p: Ezra's Ahava River appears here as "the place Thera."
b: Ezra 8:31 has "the Ahava River." Vaticanus has "the place Thera," and Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with "the river." Josephus has them set out "from Euphrates on the twelfth day of the first month" (Antiquities 11.135): the same day as here and in Ezra 8:31, but a different place. The Plain keeps the Greek name.

p: Ezra counts three days' rest and weighs the treasure on the fourth; Vaticanus makes it the third.
b: Ezra 8:32-33 says they "spent three days there. On the fourth day the silver, the gold and the vessels were weighed out." Vaticanus has "when the third day there came," and Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus adding "on the fourth day." The priest is Marmoth son of Urias, Ezra's Meremoth son of Uriah, who later repairs part of the wall (Nehemiah 3:4).

t: A thank offering for a safe journey?
p: Ezra calls the goats a sin offering; the Greek says "for deliverance" or a peace offering.
b: In Ezra 8:35 the twelve goats are a sin offering (hatta't). 1 Esdras has hyper sōtēriou, a phrase the Greek Bible uses for the shelamim, the peace offering or offering of well-being. It also means "for safety, for deliverance," which suits a people just brought safely through a dangerous road (8:60). Either way, 1 Esdras makes the arrival a thanksgiving rather than a cleansing.

p: Ezra's list of peoples ends with the Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians and Amorites; 1 Esdras has no Ammonites and ends with the Edomites.
b: The list in Ezra 9:1 joins the old Canaanite nations of Deuteronomy 7:1 with the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians of Deuteronomy 23:3-8. 1 Esdras has no Ammonites and puts Edomites (Idumaeans) for the Amorites. In unpointed Hebrew the two words are close: h'mry (הָאֱמֹרִי, "the Amorite," as in Ezra 9:1) and h'dmy ("the Edomite") share three letters, and the look-alike letters d and r stand in different places. The site's Ezra variant discusses the readings.

p: Where Ezra speaks of ma'al, breach of faith, 1 Esdras speaks of anomia, lawlessness.
b: The Hebrew ma'al (Ezra 9:2, 4; 10:2) means a breach of trust, taking what belongs to God. 1 Esdras uses anomia, "lawlessness," and its relatives (8:69, 8:87; 9:2; 9:7, "you have acted lawlessly"). The Plain keeps "lawlessness" for these words. The Greek makes the issue a breach of written law, which fits a book that ends with the law read aloud.

p: The phrase comes from Isaiah 6:13 and is used here for the people as a whole.
b: Ezra 9:2 and 1 Esdras call Israel "the holy seed," the phrase that ends Isaiah 6:13, where the stump that remains of the felled tree is "the holy seed." The idea that Israel is holy by descent, not by its priests only, underlies the demand for separation. Other biblical voices, such as Ruth and Isaiah 56:3-7, welcome foreigners who join themselves to the LORD; the topic page sets them side by side.
r: Isaiah 6:13; Ezra 9:2; Deuteronomy 7:6; Malachi 2:15; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:3-7

p: The Greek calls Ezra's robe "holy," making it a priest's garment.
b: Ezra 9:3 has "my garment and my robe" (me'il, a mantle). 1 Esdras says "the holy robe" (hiera esthēs) here and in 8:70. The change fits the book's view of Ezra as a priest, and finally as "the high priest" (9:40, 9:49). Tearing clothes and pulling out hair are signs of grief and horror, as in Job 1:20 and Nehemiah 13:25.

a: All who were stirred by the word of the Lord of Israel
p: Ezra's "those who trembled" becomes "those moved"; Alexandrinus adds "zealots."
b: Ezra 9:4 speaks of those who "trembled" (charedim) at God's word, the same group as in Ezra 10:3 and Isaiah 66:2, 5. 1 Esdras has people "stirred" or "moved" by the word. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus reading "all who were zealots, and all who were moved." Zeal for the law is the call to arms in 1 Maccabees 2:27: "Everyone who is zealous for the law and stands by the covenant, come out and follow me!"

p: Ezra confesses in the first person plural: "we," not "they."
b: Ezra's prayer (8:71-87, Ezra 9:6-15) is a classic penitential prayer, beside Nehemiah 9, Daniel 9:4-19 and Baruch 1:15-3:8. Ezra has not married a foreign wife, yet he prays "our sins." Jewish and Christian readers alike have taken the prayer as a model of standing with one's people in confession. The Greek is mostly close to the Hebrew, with small changes noted in the verses that follow.

p: The Greek agnoiai means errors made unknowingly, where the Hebrew has guilt.
b: The Hebrew of Ezra 9:6 says "our guilt is so great it reaches the heavens," using the word 'ashmah. 1 Esdras has hai agnoiai hēmōn, "our ignorances," the word the Greek law uses for sins committed unknowingly (Leviticus 5:18 in Greek). The same word comes back in 9:20, where the priests offer rams "for their error." The Greek seems to soften the guilt: the people did not know. Yet the prayer still says the sins are "great" (8:73).
orig: αἱ δὲ ἄγνοιαι ἡμῶν (hai de agnoiai hēmōn)

p: Vaticanus doubles the title here; Alexandrinus has "you, Lord."
b: Vaticanus reads para tou kyriou Kyriou, "from the Lord, Lord," and Swete's footnote gives "from you, Lord" for Alexandrinus. The doubled word is the way the Greek Bible often renders Adonai YHWH, "the Lord GOD," though Ezra 9:8 has "the LORD our God." The Plain keeps both words.

t: A root left in the ground
p: Ezra's "band of survivors" and "tent peg" become a root and a name.
b: Ezra 9:8 pictures the remnant as a group of survivors and as a tent peg driven into the holy place. 1 Esdras uses a planting image instead: God has left "a root and a name" (also 8:84, 8:85, 8:86). The root is the stump of Isaiah 6:13 and the shoot from Jesse's stump in Isaiah 11:1; the name is what lives on when a family survives (Deuteronomy 25:6).

p: Ezra's "brightened our eyes ... a little life" becomes a lamp and food.
b: Ezra 9:8 says God has "brightened our eyes and given us a little life again in our slavery." The Greek has God "uncover our light (phōstēr) in the house of our Lord" and "give us food." The light may be the temple lamp burning again, or a figure of revival, as the lamp of David in 1 Kings 11:36. The food renders the Hebrew michyah, "means of life."

a: a firm footing in Judea and Jerusalem
p: Ezra has "a fence" (gader); the Greek has stereoma, a firm place.
b: The Hebrew gader in Ezra 9:9 is a stone wall around a vineyard, a picture of protection. It may also hint at the city walls that Nehemiah will build. 1 Esdras has stereōma, "something made firm, a foundation," the word the Greek Bible uses for the "firmament" of Genesis 1:6. The sense is security, without the wall.

a: The land you go in to take possession of
p: The quotation strings together phrases from the law, not one prophet's words.
b: Ezra calls this a command given "through your servants the prophets," but no one verse says it. It joins Leviticus 18:24-28 (the land defiled by its peoples), Deuteronomy 7:3 (no marriage with them), Deuteronomy 23:6 (do not seek their peace) and Deuteronomy 11:8 (be strong and possess the land).

a: Yet again we have turned aside to break your law
p: Ezra asks, "Are we to go back to breaking your commands?"; 1 Esdras says they have done it.
b: In Ezra 9:14 Ezra asks whether the people will again break the commands and intermarry. 1 Esdras turns the question into a confession: "we have turned back again." The question about God's anger follows in 8:85, as a separate verse, and in the past tense (ouchi ōrgisthēs, "were you not angry"), where Ezra asks what God's anger would do. The KJV gives it as a possibility: "Mightest not thou be angry with us to destroy us."

p: Ezra says the LORD is tsaddiq, in the right; the Greek says alethinos, true.
b: In Ezra 9:15 the confession turns on God's justice: "you are in the right" (tsaddiq), so the punishment was deserved. 1 Esdras has alēthinos, "true, faithful," as in Exodus 34:6 in Greek. The stress moves from God's justice to his faithfulness in keeping a root alive. Coming after the contest where truth is strongest of all (4:35-41), the word has extra weight in this book.

a: Jechonias son of Jeelus, one of the Israelites
p: Ezra makes Shecaniah "of the descendants of Elam"; 1 Esdras has "of the sons of Israel."
b: The speaker in Ezra 10:2 is Shecaniah son of Jehiel, of the clan of Elam, and a Jehiel of Elam is later among those who had foreign wives (Ezra 10:26). 1 Esdras calls him Jechonias son of Jeelus, "of the sons of Israel." In Greek letters Ēlam and Israēl are not far apart, and the clan name may have been lost in copying. Josephus also calls him Jechonias, "a principal man in Jerusalem" (Antiquities 11.145).

a: But now all Israel is lifted up
p: Ezra says "there is hope for Israel"; the Greek says Israel is "above."
b: The Hebrew of Ezra 10:2 has yesh miqweh, "there is hope." The Greek has estin epanō pas Israēl, "all Israel is above," which the KJV renders "now is all Israel aloft." The meaning may be that all Israel is roused and ready, or that Israel can still rise above its sin. The Plain keeps the picture.

p: The hardest demand in the book; the text reports it without comment.
b: The proposal, as in Ezra 10:3, is to send away the foreign wives and their children. It can be read in more than one way. Read one way, it is a painful act of faithfulness by a small community that risked losing itself, as Israel had before (1 Kings 11:1-8; Nehemiah 13:26). Read another way, it goes beyond the law of Moses, which does not order foreign wives to be divorced, and stands against Ruth and Rahab, foreign women in David's line (Matthew 1:5), and against the words on divorce in Malachi 2:16 and from Jesus (Mark 10:9). The book itself reports the decision without comment. See the topic page on foreigners.
r: Ezra 10:3; Nehemiah 13:23-27; Deuteronomy 7:3-4; Malachi 2:14-16; Ruth 4:13-17; Matthew 1:5; 1 Corinthians 7:12-14

a: let us bind ourselves by oath
p: Ezra proposes a covenant; 1 Esdras an oath.
b: Ezra 10:3 says "let us make a covenant (berit) with our God." 1 Esdras uses horkōmosia, a sworn oath, which matches what Ezra then does in 8:92 (Ezra 10:5, "made ... swear"). The Greek loses the echo of Israel's covenant renewals (2 Kings 23:3; Nehemiah 10:29).

a: the room of Jonas son of Nasibus
p: Vaticanus gives the names in worn-down forms; Alexandrinus has Ezra's.
b: Ezra 10:6 says Ezra went to the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. Vaticanus has "Jonas son of Nasibus"; Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with "Joanan son of Eliasib," as in Ezra (see the variant). A high priest named Eliashib serves in Nehemiah's time (Nehemiah 3:1), and a Johanan appears later in the high priestly line (Nehemiah 12:22-23), so the names matter for dating Ezra. See the topic page.

p: Ezra repeats "went there"; 1 Esdras says he spent the night.
b: The Hebrew of Ezra 10:6 repeats "he went there," which reads awkwardly; 1 Esdras has aulistheis, "having spent the night." A small change of one letter in the Hebrew verb (wayyalen for wayyelekh) would give the Greek sense. The site's Ezra page has the variant.

a: his livestock given over to the temple
p: Ezra's "put under the ban" is rendered "consecrated" in 1 Esdras.
b: Ezra 10:8 says the absent man's goods would be cherem, "devoted," the old law of things set apart for God, sometimes by destruction (Leviticus 27:28; Joshua 6:17). 1 Esdras has anierōthēsontai ta ktēnē, "his livestock will be consecrated," that is, handed to the temple. Josephus says their substance would be "appropriated to the uses of the temple" (Antiquities 11.148), close to this Greek. The penalty is still heavy: the man is "estranged" from the community.
orig: ἀνιερωθήσονται τὰ κτήνη αὐτῶν (anierōthēsontai ta ktēnē autōn)

a: It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month
t: Winter, and a clash of months
p: The ninth month is Kislev, in winter; Josephus calls it Tebeth, which is the tenth.
b: The ninth month is Kislev (Zechariah 7:1), in the season of winter rains. Ezra 10:9 speaks of the downpours; 1 Esdras 9:6 and 9:11 speak of winter. Josephus dates the gathering to "the twentieth day of the ninth month, which, according to the Hebrews, is called Tebeth," and says the people "were uneasy because of the cold" (Antiquities 11.148-149). But Tebeth is the tenth month (Esther 2:16), so his two names for the month do not agree.

p: The Hebrew todah means both; 1 Esdras gives both Greek words.
b: The Hebrew of Ezra 10:11 says "give todah to the LORD," and todah means both "confession" and "thanks, praise" (compare Joshua 7:19, where Joshua tells Achan to give glory to the LORD and make his confession). 1 Esdras gives both senses side by side: homologian doxan, "confession, glory." The Plain keeps both.

p: Vaticanus adds three words the Hebrew does not have, and their sense is unclear.
b: After "we are not able to stand in the open," Vaticanus adds kai ouch heuromen, "and we did not find," with no object. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus without the words, and Ezra 10:13 and the KJV have nothing like them. They may mean "we found no shelter" or "we found no way," or they may be a copying slip. The Plain supplies "no way," the plainest sense; see the variant.

p: In Ezra four men oppose the plan; in 1 Esdras they carry it out.
b: Ezra 10:15 says that only Jonathan and Jahzeiah "took a stand against this," backed by Meshullam and Shabbethai. The Hebrew phrase ('amad 'al) can also mean "stood over, were in charge of," and 1 Esdras reads it that way: the men "took it on" (epedexanto), and the others "acted as umpires with them" (synebrabeusan). In 1 Esdras the community is united; in Ezra a small group protests. The KJV of Ezra 10:15 also reads it this way ("were employed about this matter"), where the site's Ezra reads opposition. The Greek verb can also mean "welcome, accept," as in 3 John 9 (epidechetai), so the men may simply have "accepted" the plan.

p: Ezra's "Shabbethai the Levite" becomes three men: Mosollamus, Levis and Sabbataeus.
b: In Ezra 10:15 Shabbethai is "the Levite." 1 Esdras turns the title into a third name, Levis, so that three men help the two leaders. A similar thing happens with Nehemiah's title at 9:49.

a: They shut themselves in to meet
p: Vaticanus says they were "shut in together"; Alexandrinus that they "sat together."
b: Ezra 10:16 says they "sat down" to examine the matter. Vaticanus has synekleisthēsan, "they were shut in together," a closed session of the court; Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with synekathisan, "they sat together," as in Ezra. The work took three months, from the tenth month to the first (9:17).

a: from the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak
p: The first names on the list come from the family of the high priest who rebuilt the temple.
b: Jeshua (Joshua) son of Jozadak was high priest with Zerubbabel (6:2; Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 3:1). That his descendants head the list shows the problem reached the top of the priesthood. Malachi charges the priests with having "ruined the covenant of Levi" (Malachi 2:8), and Judah with marrying "the daughter of a foreign god" and betraying "the wife of your youth" (Malachi 2:11, 2:14).

a: rams to make atonement for their error
p: Ezra speaks of guilt; 1 Esdras uses the word for unintentional sins again.
b: Ezra 10:19 has the priests offer "a ram from the flock for their guilt," the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14-19. 1 Esdras speaks of rams for exilasmos, "atonement," for their agnoia, "ignorance, error," the same word as in Ezra's prayer (8:72). By the law, a ram atones for sins done without knowing (Leviticus 5:18). The Greek treats the marriages as wrongs done in ignorance of the law, which the reading of the law in 9:37-55 will then remedy.
orig: ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀγνοίας αὐτῶν (hyper tēs agnoias autōn)

p: Ezra lists Immer and then Harim; 1 Esdras runs the two lists together under Emer.
b: Ezra 10:20-21 has two priestly families: Immer (Hanani, Zebadiah) and Harim (Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, Uzziah). 1 Esdras has only the heading Emer, followed by six names. The total numbers in the two lists also differ, as names were lost, added or split in copying. The Plain follows the Greek names; Ezra 10:18-43 gives the Hebrew.

a: Of the gatekeepers: Sallumus and Tolbanes
p: Vaticanus says "of the daughters"; Swete's text follows Alexandrinus's "gatekeepers."
b: Swete's footnote shows that Vaticanus itself reads thygaterōn, "daughters," and that Alexandrinus reads thyrōrōn, "gatekeepers." The two words look alike in Greek capitals. Swete prints the gatekeepers in his text, since the list is of men and Ezra 10:24 has gatekeepers. See the variant.

p: The odd name probably fuses two names from Ezra's list.
b: Ezra 10:30 lists Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui and Manasseh near the end of the family of Pahath-moab. Vaticanus has "Beskaspasmys and Sesthel and Balnus and Manasseas," and Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with Matthanias in place of Beskaspasmys. Sesthel looks like Bezalel, and Balnus like Binnui. Lists of names are where copyists went wrong most often, and the Greek and Hebrew lists here cannot be matched name for name.

p: Vaticanus has Phosepus; Alexandrinus has Josephus, as in Ezra's Joseph.
b: The last name in Ezra 10:42 is Joseph. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with Iōsēphos, Josephus, where Vaticanus has Phosēpos. The family heading Ezora and the next heading Ooma (9:35) stand where Ezra has no heading and Nebo. The Plain follows Swete's text.

a: and they sent them away with their children
t: The ending Ezra does not give
p: Ezra's last verse is hard to read; 1 Esdras says plainly that the wives and children were sent away.
b: Ezra 10:44 ends with words the site renders "Some of them had wives by whom they had had children," and the Hebrew is hard. 1 Esdras ends the list with a clear report: "and they sent them away with their children." Josephus agrees: they "cast out their wives, and the children which were born of them" (Antiquities 11.152). The book does not say whether its clear ending comes from an older Hebrew text or from the translator. Either way, 1 Esdras gives the reform a finished ending and moves straight to the reading of the law.

a: On the first day of the seventh month
t: A reading placed after the divorces
p: Nehemiah 8 sets the reading in Nehemiah's time; 1 Esdras sets it straight after Ezra 10.
b: In the Hebrew Bible the reading of the law comes in Nehemiah 7:73-8:12, years after Ezra's arrival and in the time of the governor Nehemiah. In 1 Esdras it follows directly on the marriage reform, about six months after the cases ended (9:17). The book does not say whether this is an older order of the Ezra story or an editor's choice to bring Ezra's scenes together. The Ezra and Nehemiah pages give the views; see also the chapter page.

a: in front of the temple's east gate
t: The Water Gate becomes the temple gate
p: Nehemiah places the crowd at the Water Gate; 1 Esdras before the east gate of the temple.
b: Nehemiah 8:1 gathers the people "in the open square facing the Water Gate," a city gate on the east side. 1 Esdras moves the scene to the square before the east gate of the temple. With no Nehemiah and no rebuilt walls in this book, the temple is the only center left. The reading becomes a temple event led by a priest.

p: Only 1 Esdras calls Ezra the high priest.
b: Nehemiah 8:2 calls Ezra "the priest," and Ezra 7:1-5 traces his line to Aaron, but never names him high priest. 1 Esdras calls him archiereus here and in 9:49 (Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus also at 9:39). The Hebrew books give the high priesthood to Jeshua's line, and Josephus names Joacim as "the high priest" who died "about the same time" as Ezra (Antiquities 11.158). The Greek title raises Ezra as the book's final leader, in place of the absent Nehemiah.

p: The reading is for women as well as men, as the law itself commands.
b: Both Nehemiah 8:2 and 1 Esdras stress that women heard the law, as Deuteronomy 31:12 commands for the reading every seventh year. 1 Esdras adds "all the priests" to the hearers, but leaves out Nehemiah's "everyone able to listen with understanding."

p: The Greek bema, "platform," gave its name to the bimah, the reading platform of the synagogue.
b: Nehemiah 8:4 calls it a wooden migdal, "tower." 1 Esdras has bēma, "platform, step." The bimah, the raised platform from which the Torah is read in a synagogue, takes its name from this Greek word. The site's Nehemiah page notes the same link.

a: Mattathias, Sammus, Ananias, Azarias, Urias, Ezekias and Baalsamus
p: The Greek names seven on the right and six on the left; Nehemiah has six and seven.
b: Nehemiah 8:4 names Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah on the right, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah and Meshullam on the left. The Greek adds Azarias on the right and has Ezekias (Hezekiah) and Baalsamus where Nehemiah has Hilkiah and Maaseiah; on the left it lacks Meshullam and has Lothasubus and Nabarias for Hashum and Hashbaddanah. The Plain follows the Greek.

a: the Most High God, the Almighty
p: Nehemiah says Ezra blessed the LORD; Vaticanus says Azarias did.
b: In Nehemiah 8:6 "Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God." Vaticanus has Azarias, one of the men standing at Ezra's right (9:43); Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus with Ezra, and with the longer title "the Lord God Most High, Sabaoth, the Almighty" (see the variant). The Greek title "Almighty" (Pantokratōr) is the one the Greek Bible uses for "the LORD of Armies."

p: The doubled Amen is the people's answer to the blessing.
b: "Amen" is Hebrew for "so be it, it is firm." The people answer the blessing as in Nehemiah 8:6, and as the people answer the curses in Deuteronomy 27:15-26 and the psalm in 1 Chronicles 16:36. The double Amen ends the first books of the Psalms (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19). Synagogue and church took over the custom of the people answering the leader's prayer with Amen (1 Corinthians 14:16).

a: inspiring them with the reading as they went
p: Nehemiah says the Levites explained the reading; the Greek uses a rare verb whose sense is uncertain.
b:
Nehemiah 8:8 says the Levites read "explaining it as they went." 1 Esdras has emphysiountes hama tēn anagnōsin, using a rare verb, emphysioō, that comes back in the book's last verse, where the people enephysiōthēsan by the words (9:55). Its sense is uncertain, and the Plain renders it cautiously as "inspire." The options:

"Understand." The KJV takes it as teaching for understanding: "making them withal to understand it" here, and "they understood the words" at 9:55, which matches Nehemiah's "explaining" and "grasped" (Nehemiah 8:8, 8:12).

"Inspire." The public-domain World English Bible keeps "understood" at 9:55 but gives "were inspired by" in its margin.

"Puff up, fill." The verb looks like a compound of physioō, "puff up" (1 Corinthians 8:1, "Knowledge puffs up"), so it may mean that the reading filled or lifted up the hearers. It is not the verb God uses when he breathes into the first human in Genesis 2:7 in Greek (enephysēsen, from emphysaō).

p: Katethzabdus is probably "and Jozabad," with the Greek "and" run into the name.
b: Nehemiah 8:7 lists thirteen Levites, including Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan and Pelaiah. Swete's footnote shows Alexandrinus reading "and Iozabdos" where Vaticanus has Katethzabdos, which looks like kai ("and") joined to a form of the name. The Plain keeps Vaticanus's form. The list also differs in other names: Anniuth for Bani, Sarabias for Sherebiah, Jadinus for Jamin.

t: Nehemiah's title read as a name
p: Nehemiah 8:9 has "Nehemiah, who was the governor"; 1 Esdras has a man called Attarates.
b: Nehemiah 8:9 has "Nehemiah, who was the governor" (hattirshata, a Persian title). 1 Esdras has no Nehemiah at all, and the title has become a person, Attarates (Swete's footnote gives Attharates for Alexandrinus). The same thing happened to the title in the list of returnees (5:40). Because 1 Esdras leaves out all of Nehemiah's memoir, the missing name here does not prove that the Hebrew once lacked it; the site's Nehemiah page weighs this.

a: For they were all crying as they heard the law
p: As in Nehemiah, the people weep when they hear the law, and their leaders tell them to rejoice.
b: The text does not say why they wept. In 1 Esdras the reading follows straight on the confession of 8:71-87 and the sending away of wives and children, so a reader may hear grief at what the law has cost them, or sorrow at how far the people had fallen from it (compare Josiah's reaction in 2 Kings 22:11). The leaders' answer is that a holy day is a day for joy. The site's Nehemiah page gives the other readings.

a: because the LORD will give you glory
p: Nehemiah says "the joy of the LORD is your stronghold"; 1 Esdras says "the LORD will glorify you."
b: Nehemiah 8:10 ends with a much-quoted line, "the joy of the LORD is your stronghold." 1 Esdras has "for the Lord will glorify you," which looks like a free rendering of the same Hebrew, with "joy" and "stronghold" turned into honor God will give. The promise is the same: God's favor, not grief, should mark this day.
orig: ὁ γὰρ κύριος δοξάσει ὑμᾶς (ho gar kyrios doxasei hymas)

a: to send shares to those who had nothing
p: The holy day is kept by eating well and sending food to the poor.
b: Sending portions to those who have nothing ready is a mark of joyful feasts in the Bible, as in Purim (Esther 9:19, 22) and the harvest feasts (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14). It became part of Jewish holiday custom. In Nehemiah the next day brings the discovery of the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:13-18); in 1 Esdras the book ends here.

p: 1 Esdras ends in mid-story: "and they were gathered." Is it cut off?
b:
The last Greek word, episynēchthēsan, "they were gathered together," begins a new scene, but nothing follows. In Nehemiah the next verse says the family heads "gathered to Ezra the scribe" the next day to study the law, and the Feast of Booths follows (Nehemiah 8:13-18). Three readings:

(1) The book is broken off. Bullard and Hatton's handbook says "the last sentence in the book is only a fragment" and that the book probably once had more. Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras, tells more than our text: he sets the reading of the law at the Feast of Tabernacles (Antiquities 11.154), tells of eight days in booths (11.157), and ends with Ezra's death and burial in Jerusalem (11.158). But his order is not this book's, so he does not show what a longer copy contained.

(2) The ending was meant (Claude's reading). The book began with a feast (Josiah's Passover, 1:1-20) and ends with a feast of joy; a gathering of the people around the law would be a fitting close. This is offered as a possibility, not as a published view.

(3) The clause belongs with what comes before. The KJV takes it that way: "for the which they had been assembled."
